title: Geotechnical Survey Before Building a House: Needed and How?
desc: What a geotechnical survey is, whether a house should have one, what it involves, what the report contains, and when to consider it carefully.
summary: An explanation of geotechnical surveys for houses: the benefits, when to do one, the basic process and how to read the survey report.
body: p

Many owners skip the geotechnical survey because they think “a small house does not need it”. In fact, geology is the most important input for the engineer choosing the foundation. This article explains what a geotechnical survey is, when to do one and how to work with the survey firm.
h2
1. What is a geotechnical survey?
p

Under Article 21 of the Construction Law 2025, construction survey includes topographic survey; engineering geological and hydrogeological survey; hydrological survey; survey of the existing condition of works; and other survey work. For a house, an engineering geological survey usually consists of drilling to take soil samples at several points and carrying out field and laboratory tests to learn the soil layers below, their density, bearing capacity and the groundwater level.
h2
2. Does a single-family house need a survey?
p

The law does not separately list a survey obligation for each house, but it requires the design and construction of single-family houses to comply with technical standards and regulations and to ensure safety for people, property and neighbouring works (Clause 1, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). To design the foundation correctly you must know the ground. A survey is especially advisable in these cases:
ul
The plot used to be a pond, lake, paddy field, ditch or dump, or has recently been filled.
A house with many floors, a basement or a large load.
Close to an old adjoining house showing cracks or settlement.
An area where neighbouring houses have already settled or tilted.
No reliable geological information for the area.
h2
3. What requirements must a survey meet?
p

Under Article 22 of the Construction Law 2025, the survey task and technical plan must suit the type and grade of the work and the design requirements; comply with the regulations and standards on surveying; and the results must be set out in an honest, objective report that reflects the real situation. The survey contractor must propose supplementing the task when it finds factors that directly affect the design solution, and is responsible for the survey results (Article 37).
h2
4. The survey process for a house
ol
The design engineer prepares or comments on the survey task: number of boreholes, expected depth and tests required, suited to the scale of the house.
Choose a capable survey firm and sign a contract that clearly states the scope of work and the report submission time.
Drilling and sampling are carried out on site; the owner should be present or appoint someone to supervise.
Receive the survey report and pass it to the structural engineer to select and calculate the foundation.
h2
5. Reading the survey report: what should owners look at?
ul
Geological section: the order of the soil layers, which are weak (mud, soft plastic clay, fill) and which are good and at what depth.
Groundwater level: affects foundation excavation, basements and waterproofing.
Survey firm's recommendations: suitable foundation types and points to note during construction.
Borehole locations: whether they are within your plot and represent the whole plot.
p

The survey cost is usually small compared with the total cost of building a house, but it can help avoid an over-built foundation (wasting money) or an under-built one (settlement and cracks). Quan Construction can help prepare the survey task and read the results - contact Quan Construction.
note

This article is for reference; every work needs to be surveyed and designed by a qualified person. The principles above do not replace the drawings, technical instructions and calculations of the structural engineer for each specific house.
